transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

Um, hi. Yeah, thanks. So, I came in because I went from... well, barely settling into my new apartment. Which, honestly, the move was a complete nightmare. The movers actually chipped my favorite standing desk, and it’s this really specific bamboo finish that I can't just paint over, you know? I spent like three hours watching YouTube tutorials on how to fix bamboo veneer. 

But anyway, I went from just trying to unpack my boxes there to suddenly saying yes to all these mentoring sessions. And I started taking on extra client prototypes, plus I decided I needed to redesign my entire portfolio from scratch. It was like I had to fix my whole life in one sprint. 

Sprints are what we use in web design, like agile methodology? Though honestly, my project manager just uses it as an excuse to micromanage us on Slack. He's always messaging me asking about wireframes for the new interface, which is just... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right. Yeah, I just started taking on a ton of stuff out of nowhere.
During this time, did you feel unusually high or overly excited compared with your normal self?

Um, yeah, I guess so? Earlier this month I felt almost... electric. Just super upbeat and buzzing. Which is funny because the actual electricity in my new apartment is a total disaster. Half the outlets in the kitchen don't even work, and I had to buy this massive, heavy-duty extension cord just to plug in my espresso machine. Which, by the way, if you don't descale those things every three months, the pressure valve completely clogs up. I had to order this special German descaling powder on Amazon just to fix it. 

But anyway, yeah, I was feeling really electric and upbeat one minute, but then... I don't know, I'd just snap. Like, I completely snapped at this backend contractor at work, and my sister, too. She was supposed to bring over her power drill so I could mount my monitors—because working on a single laptop screen is terrible for your cervical spine, I read this whole ergonomic study about it—and she was like maybe ten minutes late because of traffic on the interstate. They've been doing construction on her exit since like 2019, so I should have known, but I just lost it on her. 

It was over these tiny delays, but in my head, it felt like they were personally trying to block me from getting all my stuff done. I don't know why I reacted like that.
During that upbeat, buzzing period, did you need less sleep than usual?

Yeah, definitely. For like, several nights in a row, I was getting maybe three or four hours of sleep. Tops. And the weird thing is, I'd wake up and feel totally fine, like, convinced I was perfectly rested and I should just use the extra time to get ahead on everything. 

Which honestly, mornings are usually the worst for me because I'm super particular about my coffee. I have this whole pour-over setup, the Chemex one? It's the glass one with the wooden collar. But the filters are so expensive, and you have to fold them in this very specific way or the water channels weirdly and ruins the extraction. I actually watched this whole documentary on coffee bean processing in Ethiopia, and it turns out the washing stations there use a completely different fermentation method than they do in Colombia. It really affects the acidity profile. 

But yeah, I'd just wake up at like 3 AM, completely wired, thinking about all the design mockups I could finish before the sun even came up.
During that buzzing period, did you have any experiences where your thoughts or perceptions felt out of touch with reality?

Out of touch with reality? Um, no, I don't think so. I mean, my thoughts were moving super fast, but I always knew what was real. I wasn't seeing things or, like, believing crazy conspiracies or anything. 

Though speaking of reality, virtual reality is getting so intense right now. We were looking into doing some VR interfaces for a client, and I had to test out this headset. It actually made me super nauseous. Apparently, there's this disconnect between your vestibular system and what your eyes are seeing, and it causes motion sickness. My friend who works in game design told me they have to use these specific frame rates just to keep people from throwing up. He actually moved to Seattle for that job, which is crazy because it rains there like nine months out of the year. I could never deal with that much gray weather, I need natural light for my plants. I have this Monstera that's taking over my living room, and if it doesn't get enough indirect sunlight, the leaves don't get those cool splits in them. 

But no, to answer your question, I was definitely grounded in reality. Just... moving through it a lot faster than everyone else, I guess.
During that buzzing period, were you hospitalized because of how you were acting or feeling?

Hospitalized? Um, no. No, definitely not. I didn't go to a hospital or anything. 

I actually really hate hospitals. The last time I had to go to one was when my mom had knee surgery, and I was just appalled by the patient portal app they made her use to check her discharge paperwork. The user interface was a complete nightmare. The navigation menu was buried under this tiny hamburger icon that didn't even have a bounding box, so older users would have absolutely no idea it was clickable. I actually wrote a whole Medium article about accessibility in healthcare UX after that. Accessibility is getting so overlooked lately, especially with everyone rushing to push out mobile apps without doing proper user testing. Like, you can't just assume everyone has perfect vision and fine motor control, you know? 

But, um... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right. No, I wasn't in a hospital. I was just working a lot from my apartment.
During that buzzing period, did it cause serious problems in your life or work?

Um... yeah, I guess it did. I actually completely missed a major design review at work. Which is awful, I never do that. We usually do our reviews in Figma, and they just rolled out this new update with advanced prototyping, which is amazing for micro-interactions, but it uses so much RAM. My MacBook sounded like it was going to take off like a jet engine. I really need to upgrade to one of the new chips, but Apple's pricing tiers for unified memory are just borderline extortion. Like, charging that much for an extra eight gigs of RAM in this economy? It's ridiculous. I watched a whole teardown video of the new laptops, and the architecture is fascinating, but still.

But, um... anyway, yeah, I missed the review. And honestly, I've been avoiding my friends and family, too. I just feel so embarrassed about how scattered and unreliable I’ve seemed lately. I just kind of ghosted everyone. My sister kept texting me, and I couldn't even look at my phone. The notifications were just piling up. I actually put my phone in grayscale mode because I read it makes you less addicted to the screen, but it just made all my app icons look really depressing. Color theory is so important for mood, you know? Like, there's a reason fast food places use red and yellow, it literally triggers urgency and hunger. 

But yeah... I've just been avoiding everyone because I'm embarrassed about how all over the place I've been.
Before this recent buzzing period, have you ever had a time lasting at least two weeks when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Um, yeah. Actually, lately it's been exactly like that. I wake up with this heavy, gray feeling in my chest, and even when the apartment is totally quiet and nothing bad is happening at all, I feel like I could just cry over a coffee mug left in the sink. 

Speaking of mugs, I actually have this huge collection of handmade ceramics. I used to buy them all on Etsy, but honestly, Etsy's search algorithm has gotten so terrible lately. It's completely flooded with dropshippers now. You try to filter for actual handmade items, and the UI just feeds you page after page of mass-produced stuff. It totally ruins the user journey. E-commerce platforms really need better tagging systems, but they probably don't care because they get their transaction fee either way. It's like how every website now has those aggressive modal pop-ups for newsletter signups before you can even scroll down the page. Dark patterns in UX just drive me insane, they're so hostile to the user. Like, let me read the content first before you demand my email address! 

But um... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right. Feeling depressed. Yeah, that heavy, gray feeling has been pretty constant for a while now. Just feeling down most of the day.
When you were feeling electric and sleeping only a few hours, were you also feeling depressed at the same time?

Um, no, definitely not. When I was feeling all buzzing and electric, I wasn't down at all. I was just... going. Like I had a million tabs open in my brain and they were all loading perfectly. 

Actually, speaking of being electric, I ended up buying all these smart LED bulbs for my apartment during that time because I decided the ambient lighting was completely wrong for my productivity. I got the ones that sync with your monitor, which sounds amazing for immersive design work, but the companion app is a total disaster. The color wheel for selecting the hue is completely non-responsive. You drag your finger to a warm amber, and it snaps back to this harsh, clinical blue. It’s a basic touch-target issue! And they force you to create an account just to turn on a lamp. I really hate how every IoT device now requires a login. It’s just blatant data harvesting. Like, why does a lightbulb need my precise location data? It's a massive privacy violation, and the privacy policy was just a wall of unformatted legal text with zero hierarchy. 

But, um... sorry, I got distracted. What did you ask? Oh, right, was I depressed at the same time. No, no. That heavy, sad feeling didn't happen then. They were like completely different modes. I definitely wasn't both at once.
About how many days did that buzzing, high-energy period last?

Um, let's see... the buzzing period. Well, this whole intense up-and-down pattern, the high energy and then the crash, it's basically been going on since I moved into this new apartment about a month ago. 

Actually, the move was a total nightmare. I hired this moving company because their website looked so clean and modern—lots of whitespace, really nice sans-serif typography, you know? It gave off this vibe of being super professional and organized. But their actual service was chaos. The booking portal didn't even have a calendar integration, so I had to manually email back and forth to confirm the date. And then on moving day, they scratched my vintage credenza. It just goes to show that a good UI doesn't necessarily mean a good backend operation. It's like when an app has a beautiful onboarding flow but the core functionality is completely buggy. You can't just slap a nice coat of paint on a broken system. I actually left them a review and suggested they implement a better scheduling API, but I doubt they even read it. 

But um... yeah, so the whole up-and-down thing has been happening for about a month, since I moved in.
How many days in a row did that buzzing, high-energy period last?

Um, how many days in a row? Gosh, I'm not totally sure exactly how many days it was continuous. I just know the whole back-and-forth thing has been happening for a month. 

I really should have been tracking it in my bullet journal, but honestly, I've completely abandoned analog tracking lately. I tried switching to this new habit-tracking app that everyone on design Twitter was raving about, but the micro-interactions are just so overdone. Every time you check off a task, there's this massive confetti animation that takes up the whole screen and blocks you from tapping the next item. It's like, okay, I get it, positive reinforcement, but you're adding friction to the core user flow! I ended up submitting a bug report about the animation duration, but they just closed it as "working as intended." It's so frustrating when developers prioritize flashy UI over actual usability. Like, just give me a clean checklist with a satisfying haptic feedback, you know? 

But, um, sorry, what did you ask? Oh, the days in a row. Yeah, I really don't know the exact number of days for just the buzzing part. I didn't keep track of it like that.
Did that buzzing, high-energy period last for at least 7 days in a row?

Um, seven days? I mean, maybe? I really couldn't tell you if it was exactly a week straight. Time gets kind of blurry when I'm like that. 

Actually, speaking of time getting blurry, I was looking at my screen time stats on my phone the other day, and the data visualization they use is just... it's honestly embarrassing. They use these stacked bar charts for app categories, but the colors they chose for "Productivity" and "Social" are practically identical if you have your screen brightness turned down even a little bit. It's a huge accessibility failure. I don't understand how a company that big can release a dashboard without running it through a basic contrast checker. And don't even get me started on the way they handle the weekly averages—the tooltip hover state is so sensitive that you can't even read the exact minutes before it snaps to the next day. I spent like an hour trying to redesign the interface in Figma just to prove to myself that it could be done better. I was going to post it on Dribbble, but then I got sidetracked organizing my font library. 

But um, wait, what were we talking about? Oh, the seven days thing. Yeah, I'm honestly not sure. It could have been seven days, or maybe less? I just know it was part of that whole month-long mess since I moved.
During that buzzing, high-energy period, did your symptoms make it impossible for you to function normally at work or in your daily life?

Um, impossible to function? Well, it definitely messed things up. I actually missed a really important design review at work because I was just... I don't even know, my brain was in a million places. 

And speaking of design reviews, the tool we use for remote collaboration is just a nightmare. They recently pushed an update that completely broke the comment threading. So now, if a stakeholder leaves feedback on a specific frame, the reply chain gets detached if you zoom out too far. It's infuriating! I spent half of yesterday just trying to piece together a conversation between our lead developer and the product manager because their comments were floating in the middle of nowhere on the canvas. It's like, did they even do user testing before rolling this out? You can't just disrupt the core workflow of a collaborative tool and expect people to just adapt. I was so annoyed I almost wrote a medium article about the decline of QA in enterprise software. 

But um, yeah, so I missed that review, which was bad. And honestly, I've been avoiding my friends and family too. I just feel so embarrassed about how scattered and unreliable I've seemed lately. It's like I can't keep anything straight.
During that buzzing, high-energy period, did you get into serious trouble at work or in your daily life because of it?

Um, serious trouble? I mean, like I just said, I missed that huge design review, which is pretty bad for my job. And I've just been totally dodging my friends and my family because I'm just... I'm so embarrassed about how scattered and, I don't know, unreliable I've been acting. 

It's actually kind of like how I've been avoiding opening my email inbox. They switched us to this new email client at work, and the typography is just offensive. I'm not even exaggerating. They're using a sans-serif font for the body text, but the kerning is so tight that the 'r' and 'n' constantly look like an 'm'. It makes reading long threads physically exhausting. I don't know who thought it was a good idea to prioritize this brutalist aesthetic over basic legibility. I actually started drafting a proposal to the IT department to let us switch back to the old client, or at least let us inject custom CSS, but then I realized I didn't even have the energy to finish writing it. 

But um, yeah, what was the question? Oh, serious trouble. Yeah, missing the review and ghosting everyone... it's definitely causing problems for me.
Did the buzzing, high-energy period last for at least 4 days in a row?

Um, four days? I... yeah, I guess it could have been four days. That sounds a little more realistic than a whole week, but I still can't say for sure. Time tracking just wasn't happening. 

Which, honestly, is ironic because I'm usually obsessed with time-tracking apps. I downloaded this new one last week that promised to use AI to auto-categorize your tasks, but the UI is a complete disaster. They decided to use this dark mode theme with neon green accents, which, fine, maybe they're going for a cyberpunk vibe. But the contrast ratio on the secondary text is like 2:1. It's completely illegible! And the animation when you complete a task takes a full 1.5 seconds. Do you know how much friction that adds when you're trying to quickly log a bunch of micro-tasks? I actually started decompiling the app just to see if I could speed up the animation duration in the code, but I got distracted looking at their icon assets. They're not even using SVGs for everything, which is just lazy. 

But um, what were you asking? Oh, four days. Yeah, I don't know for sure. It's definitely possible, but I really wasn't keeping track of how long it lasted.
During that buzzing period, did you get fired, suspended, or receive a formal warning at work because of your behavior?

Um, fired or suspended? No, nothing official like that. I mean, like I mentioned, I missed that big design review, which was awful, and I've been hiding from my friends and family because I'm just so embarrassed about being so scattered and unreliable. 

But no formal warnings. Although, speaking of warnings, I keep getting these automated alert emails from our cloud storage provider because we're nearing our data cap, and the way they designed the alert banner is just a crime against user experience. It's this massive, aggressive red bar that pushes the entire interface down by like 50 pixels every time you log in. And there's no way to dismiss it permanently! You click the little 'x', and it just comes back the next session. It completely breaks the spatial memory of where the navigation elements are supposed to be. I actually spent three hours on a Saturday trying to write a custom browser extension just to block the specific div class for that banner because I couldn't handle the visual disruption anymore. It's like these companies don't even consider cognitive load when they design these intrusive notifications. 

But um, wait, what did you ask? Oh, right, fired or suspended. No, no formal warnings or anything like that. Just the missed review and me feeling too embarrassed to face anyone.
Did the heavy, gray depressed feeling start only after the buzzing, high-energy period ended?

Um, start only after the buzzing ended? No, no, the heavy, gray feeling... that's been around for a while. The heavier depressive stretches have been showing up since my separation about 11 months ago. That was way before this latest move made everything sharper and weirder. 

Which, speaking of moving, trying to update my address across all my accounts has been an absolute nightmare of form design. You wouldn't believe how many major institutions still use drop-down menus for the state field without enabling keystroke navigation. I was trying to update my billing info for my domain registrar, and I had to manually scroll past 40 states just to click on mine. And don't even get me started on the zip code validation. They had it set to reject anything with a dash, so my ZIP+4 wouldn't go through, but there was no inline error message! Just a generic 'form submission failed' at the top of the page after the reload, which meant I had to re-enter my password. It's like they're actively trying to increase their bounce rate. I actually started inspecting the page source to see if they were using some archaic jQuery validation plugin from 2012, and sure enough... 

But um, wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, the gray feeling. Yeah, it didn't just start after the buzzing. It's been coming and going since the separation 11 months ago.
At any point in your life, have you ever had a period when you felt unusually high or energized that lasted at least 7 days in a row?

Um, seven days in a row? No, I don't think so. I've never had a stretch like that last a full week. Like I said before, it was probably closer to four days for this last one, but definitely not seven. 

Which is honestly a relief because I don't think my laptop battery could handle a seven-day stretch of me hyper-focusing. Speaking of which, I finally decided to upgrade my workstation setup last week, and the checkout flow on this custom PC builder site was just... baffling. They had this multi-step accordion form, which is fine in theory, but they didn't implement any state saving. So if you accidentally clicked outside the modal to check a spec on another tab, the entire form reset. All your custom component selections, just gone. And they used this really aggressive CSS transition on the accordion panels that made the whole page judder every time you opened a new section. I was so frustrated I almost emailed their lead designer with a wireframe of how they could fix it using local storage and a smoother easing function. It's just basic usability principles, you know? 

But um, what was the question? Oh, a full seven days. No, no, I've never had that happen for a whole week. Just the shorter bursts.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there were psychotic features during the elevated mood period, which would help distinguish bipolar I mania from hypomania and ADHD.
doctor.question: During that buzzing period, did you have any experiences where your thoughts or perceptions felt out of touch with reality?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychotic symptoms (thoughts or perceptions out of touch with reality), which are not included in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Out of touch with reality? Um, no, I don't think so. I mean, my thoughts were moving super fast, but I always knew what was real. I wasn't seeing things or, like, believing crazy conspiracies or anything.
